questions.question: What is the main purpose of designing products using the principles of Design for Disassembly (DfD) and Design for Recycling (DfR)?

options.A: To make products cheaper to produce in the first place.
options.B: To make products last longer before they break down.
options.C: To easily take products apart and reuse their materials at the end of their life.
options.D: To use only natural, organic materials in all products.

questions.explanation: DfD and DfR focus on making products easy to separate into components so their materials can be recovered and given new life, rather than being thrown away.

questions.question: How does designing products for disassembly and recycling connect with biblical principles, as discussed in the lesson?

options.A: It shows that humans are superior to God's creation and can do whatever they want with resources.
options.B: It encourages us to be wasteful so we can buy new things and support the economy.
options.C: It reflects God's plan for preservation and renewal, encouraging us to be wise stewards of His resources.
options.D: It proves that all materials are meant to last forever without changing or being reused.

questions.explanation: The lesson connects DfD and DfR to God's example of preservation and renewal, emphasizing our role as wise stewards of the resources He provides.

questions.question: Which of these product design choices would make a cell phone *hardest* to disassemble and recycle at the end of its life?

options.A: Using standardized screws for all major components.
options.B: Connecting different materials with strong, permanent glue.
options.C: Designing modular components that snap together without tools.
options.D: Clearly labeling different material types on each part.

questions.explanation: Strong adhesives create permanent bonds between materials, making them very difficult to separate without damage, which hinders both disassembly and recycling.

questions.question: If you are using the Objective, Constraint, Variable (OCV) method to design a new school chair with Design for Disassembly in mind, which of the following would be your *Objective*?

options.A: Using only wood and metal for the chair's construction.
options.B: Making sure the chair costs less than $50 to produce.
options.C: Designing the chair so its parts can be easily separated and reused at the end of its life.
options.D: Deciding whether to use screws or snap-fits for connections.

questions.explanation: The Objective in OCV is the main goal you are trying to achieve, and for DfD, that goal is to make the product easy to take apart for material recovery.

questions.question: When thinking about Design for Disassembly, how does understanding 'multiscale modeling' help Creationeers™?

options.A: It helps us understand how a product's color changes over time.
options.B: It shows how easily a product can be taken apart (macro-level) is affected by how its materials are joined at a tiny level (atomic-level).
options.C: It explains why some products are more expensive than others.
options.D: It helps us decide which factories should build the product.

questions.explanation: Multiscale modeling connects the visible ease of disassembly (macro-level) to the underlying material connections, like atomic bonds from glue versus mechanical fasteners, which is crucial for DfD.
